title: The people hiding in our words
text: Everyday English {{1}} smuggled hundreds of people into our speech. The sandwich {{2}} after an earl {{3}} hunger for uninterrupted cards turned bread-and-filling into a word; the boycott {{4}} Captain Boycott, an Irish land agent whose tenants simply refused to deal with him; and milk is pasteurised {{5}} the process Louis Pasteur developed. Physicists left {{6}} names in every socket in the world: the volt, the ampere and the watt. Once you notice the smuggled people, you begin to find them {{7}}, and each discovery is a small lesson in the history {{8}} inside a word.

gaps.explanation: Present perfect with a singular subject: has smuggled.

gaps.hint: participle: the sandwich ___ after an earl
gaps.explanation: Reduced passive: the sandwich named after an earl.

gaps.hint: relative: an earl ___ hunger for cards
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' links the earl to his hunger.
'Named after' — the source of the word takes 'after'.
Passive agent: pasteurised by the process.
The names belong to the physicists: their names.
The discoveries appear in every place: everywhere.

gaps.hint: participle: the history ___ inside a word
gaps.explanation: Reduced relative: the history hiding inside a word.
